thread.title: Apple: Too Big To Miss - Apple Inc. AAPL)

author: Michael Wiggins De Oliveira
title: Apple: Too Big To Miss - Apple Inc. AAPL)
text:
Investment Thesis Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) is my number one pick amongst all of the large-cap tech stocks. Investors don't need to be the smartest on the Street, just savvy enough to make one decision to buy and the second decision to do nothing and wait 3-5 years. Easy returns.
Recent Developments Apple came up with the idea of growing its Services segment at the back end of 2016. At the time, the goal was set; it was to double its Services business so that by 2021 it would be "the size of a standalone Fortune 100 company".
How has it fared so far? Pretty remarkably, if you ask me. For instance, as of Q1 2018, Apple's Services business had grown an astonishing 31% YoY to $9.2 billion (15% of the company’s total revenue). If Apple’s Services were a standalone, free cash flow-generative business, growing at 31% YoY, how much would investors be willing to pay up for it? It is difficult to say for sure, as there are not so many companies, which are asset-light and growing at 30% a year with $40 billion of revenue.
However, for the purposes of our discussion, whilst not particularly free cash flow-generative, but certainly targeting the same demographic of consumers, I mused over Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ). Netflix is obviously not asset-light (contrary to popular, but wrong, belief), and it only has $12 billion of revenue in a full year; however, investors are willing to pay more than $150 billion market cap for Netflix - is there a conglomerate discount in Apple?
Ironically, Netflix considers Apple's venture into programming content as a potential competitor . And so it should. For example, Apple is rumoured to be spending around $4.2 billion into original content by 2022. On the one hand, this number is significantly smaller than Netflix's $8 billion for 2018 alone. On the other hand, while Netflix boasts of 125 million subscribers, Apple already has 48 million subscribers , and this is not even the main revenue stream for the company (iPhone sales bring in 63% of Apple’s total revenue). Long story short, I contend that there is hidden value not being fully accounted for in Apple’s Services.
Share Repurchases When the news first came out about the share repurchases , that was all the investment community was focused on at first. However, recently, I don’t see much discussion about the $100 billion announced share repurchases. How could investors have forgotten this already? CFO Maestri did not mince words. He argued on the earnings call that Apple was, in his opinion, undervalued and that the company would be looking to deploy large amounts of capital, to the benefit of long-term shareholders.

I have included Netflix as a peer to Apple, which it is not really. At least not directly. However, where Netflix could have some overlap with Apple in its business model is one of recurring revenue from subscribers who wish to get content on demand. And that is what I have tried to highlight in the above article - that Apple is pivoting away from ad hoc sales to consumers and towards a subscriber-based model.
Moreover, importantly, Netflix is also included in the above table to exemplify what I humbly believe to be a bubble, yet in comparison how Apple is far from trading anywhere near overvalued. For example, whereas Netflix's P/S is headed towards 13X, Apple is at 4X its P/S. On the other hand, one could undoubtedly argue that Apple is not growing as fast as Netflix either.
Takeaway According to a finding reported in The Little Book of Behavioral Investing by James Montier, over the past 20 years (the book was published in 2010), the S&P 500 (NYSEARCA: SPY ) generated just over 8%, whilst active managers, after fees, deliver to investors between 6% and 7% in returns. However, equity fund investors have only managed to get around 1.9% per year. Why the discrepancy? It boils down to buying and selling at the worst possible times. Essentially, timing the market rather than time spent in the market.
With Apple, I reason that it has a bright future ahead, but investors are not being asked to pay up for any such optimism. Buying Apple for 3-5 years is likely to emerge as a most rewarding investment.
